title: Symposium
author: Plato
openingText: And now I will tell you the reason why, and what the original nature of man was, and the great change which was made in him. The sexes were not two as they are now, but originally three in number; there was man, woman, and the union of the two, having a name corresponding to this double nature, which had once a real existence, but is now lost, though a word of ill omen.
about:
The Symposium is a dialogue about love. Six men at a drinking party take turns making speeches in praise of Eros — each from a different angle: poetic, political, comic, philosophical. The most famous speech is Aristophanes's: humans were originally double creatures, split by the gods, and ever since each of us looks for our other half. Socrates speaks last, with a different account.

Plato wrote it in mid-career. It is one of the most read of his dialogues partly because it is also a great piece of writing — the comedy is real, the philosophy escalates, and the final entrance of the drunken Alcibiades reframes everything that came before. It has shaped how the West has thought about love for two thousand years.

angleCards.title: What love actually is.
angleCards.text: Diotima's ladder — from physical attraction to the Form of Beauty — is one of the strangest and most ambitious arguments in all of philosophy. I want to follow it carefully and see whether it holds.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand what love actually is — I'm following Diotima's ladder from physical attraction up toward the Form of Beauty itself, and asking whether Plato's account is more convincing than Aristophanes' myth.

angleCards.title: Eros as a philosophical problem.
angleCards.text: Why does Plato take erotic longing seriously as a route to wisdom? I want to understand what distinguishes Eros from friendship, duty, or affection — and what Plato thinks it is actually pointing toward.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading the Symposium to understand the difference between Eros and other kinds of love — why Plato treats erotic longing as philosophically significant rather than just a feeling.

angleCards.title: Alcibiades and the limits of philosophy.
angleCards.text: His speech is the most personal thing in all of Plato — a confession from a man who knew exactly what he should do and chose otherwise. I want to understand what that tells us about the gap between knowledge and action.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm most interested in Alcibiades' speech about Socrates — it's the most personal thing in all of Plato, and I want to understand what it reveals about the limits of philosophy and the gap between knowing the good and choosing it.

angleCards.title: Why the myth is wrong.
angleCards.text: Aristophanes' speech is the most memorable in the dialogue — the story of humans split in two. But Plato includes it precisely because he thinks it's the most seductive error. I want to understand why Plato rejects it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading the Symposium to understand why Aristophanes' myth — that lovers are split halves searching for each other — is so persuasive and yet, in Plato's view, fundamentally wrong about what love is for.

cast.name: Socrates
cast.description: Won't give his own speech — reports Diotima's instead. Arrives unusually clean, listens to everyone, then dismantles every previous argument without appearing to try.

cast.name: Alcibiades
cast.description: The most gifted and most disastrous Athenian of his generation. Crashes the party and gives the most honest speech — about what it is like to love someone you cannot become.

cast.name: Aristophanes
cast.description: Tells the myth of split souls — the most memorable speech despite being, in Plato's view, the most philosophically seductive error. His theory is still the most popular account of romantic love in the Western world.

cast.name: Diotima
cast.description: The wise woman Socrates quotes at length. Never physically present. In a dialogue full of men praising love, the deepest view belongs to the one person not in the room.

cast.name: Phaedrus
cast.description: The one who suggested the evening's theme. His opening speech praises love as a source of courage — the lover who will die for the beloved. Earnest, honourable, the least wrong of the early speakers.

cast.name: Agathon
cast.description: A celebrated tragic poet celebrating his own victory. Gives the most beautiful speech — and, Socrates will gently show, the most empty one. Rhetoric mistaken for argument.

whyItMatters.title: Six Theories of Love
whyItMatters.body: The dialogue is structured as competing accounts. Each speech is a serious attempt to say what love is — for the beloved, for the city, for beauty, for the divine. Reading the Symposium is reading the founding catalog of what love has meant in the West.

whyItMatters.title: The Aristophanes Speech
whyItMatters.body: The story of humans as halves of original double beings, looking for our other half — that's where it comes from. The image has become a permanent part of how romantic love gets imagined.

whyItMatters.title: Socrates and the Ladder of Beauty
whyItMatters.body: Socrates, attributing his speech to a priestess named Diotima, describes love as a ladder: starting from one beautiful body, ascending to all bodies, then to souls, then to laws, then to knowledge, then to beauty itself. The argument is the founding text of Platonic love.
